title: Is Now a Good Time to Buy a Home in Middle Tennessee?
description: Is now a good time to buy? A plain look at Nashville-area market numbers, mortgage rates and personal readiness, without predictions about prices or rates.
keyword: is now a good time to buy
body:
Almost every buyer I talk with asks some version of the same question: is now a good time to buy? I can't answer that for you, and nobody can answer it for the whole market. What I can do is show you what the local numbers say today, what they don't say, and how to think about the decision for your own situation.

This post doesn't predict where prices or rates are headed. Nobody can do that reliably.

## What the local numbers show

{{img:0}}

Start with the most recent data. For the Nashville metro area, the four weeks ending 2026-09-27, [Redfin's data](https://www.redfin.com/news/data-center/) shows a median sale price of $462,304, a median of 68 days on market, and homes selling for 97.8% of list price on average. There were 2,489 homes sold in that window.

The broader Nashville numbers, a rolling three months as of 2026-08-31, point the same way. Redfin reported a median sale price of $477,500, down 0.1% from a year earlier. Median days on market was 64, the average sale-to-list ratio was 97.6%, and there were 4,850 active listings.

In plain terms, homes are taking a couple of months to sell, and buyers are, on average, paying a little under asking price. Prices look roughly flat compared with last year.

## What months of supply says

Months of supply is how long it would take to sell every active listing at the current pace of sales. Under 4 months favors sellers, 4 to 6 months is balanced, and over 6 months favors buyers.

Redfin shows 5.3 months for Nashville as of 2026-08-31, and 5.4 months for the metro area in the four weeks ending 2026-09-27. Both sit inside the balanced range, in the upper half of it.

Other sources lean the same direction. [Zillow Research](https://www.zillow.com/research/data/) had its Market Temperature Index for Nashville at 44, which it describes as leaning toward buyers, and the index was down 6 points over three months. That signals a cooling trend. Realtor.com Research put Davidson County's hotness score at 16.6 out of 100.

These are snapshots of the past. They tell you how conditions feel now, not what they will do next.

## Mortgage rates and your monthly payment

{{img:1}}

For many buyers, the rate matters more than the price. Freddie Mac's 30-year fixed average was 7.28% for the week of 2026-10-01, according to Freddie Mac data on FRED.

A rate that high raises the monthly payment on any loan amount. You can see the effect with your own numbers in the [mortgage calculator](/mortgage-calculator). Try a few prices and down payments, and add taxes and insurance, because the principal and interest payment is only part of the monthly cost.

Many buyers wait for rates to fall. That is a bet, and it can go either direction. Waiting also has costs that are easy to overlook: rent you keep paying, price changes, and losing a home you wanted.

## If rates worry you, know the options

There are a few ways buyers work with a higher rate. None is a guarantee, and a lender has to confirm what applies to your loan.

- **Refinance later.** Some buyers buy now and refinance if rates fall. That depends on rates, credit, home value and income at that time, and a refinance has its own closing costs. Treat it as a possibility, not a plan.
- **Ask about seller concessions.** You can ask the seller to pay some closing costs or to fund a temporary or permanent rate buydown. Whether that works depends on the seller, the home and the market.
- **Look at an adjustable-rate mortgage.** An ARM has a rate that is fixed for an initial period and can then change. It may lower the early payment but carries the risk of higher payments later. The CFPB has plain-language guides at [Owning a Home](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/owning-a-home/).
- **Ask about assumable loans.** Some existing FHA and VA loans can be taken over by a qualified buyer with lender approval. They are uncommon, so ask but don't count on finding one.

The Tennessee Housing Development Agency also offers home loan programs through participating lenders. You can read about them at [THDA](https://www.thda.org) and ask any lender whether they take part.

## Your readiness matters more than the calendar

Some buyers try to time the seasons. Listings and buyer activity do vary through the year, but the right moment for one household usually depends more on its own finances, timeline and the specific home than on the calendar.

A more useful set of questions looks at you:

- Is your income stable?
- Will you still have an emergency fund after closing?
- Does the payment fit comfortably in your monthly budget?
- How long do you expect to stay in the home?

Budget for the cash needed up front, too. Closing costs typically run 2 to 4 percent of the purchase price, plus earnest money and moving costs. On a conventional loan with less than 20 percent down, private mortgage insurance is typically required. Many buyers put down less than 20 percent, and several loan programs allow smaller down payments. FHA loans allow as little as 3.5 percent down, and VA loans typically require no down payment.

Another way to frame it is to compare the full monthly cost of buying (payment, taxes, insurance, maintenance) with the monthly cost of renting a comparable home. Then weigh that against how long you plan to stay.

## Look at your own city and price range

Metro numbers are an average. Conditions can differ a lot between cities, price ranges and neighborhoods. Months of supply, days on market and sale-to-list ratio for the place you want to buy tell you more than a national headline.

Geography matters too. Spring Hill includes parts of both Williamson and Maury counties, so county services, schools and taxes can differ by address. Murfreesboro is in Rutherford County and Columbia is in Maury County, and neither is in Williamson County. Property taxes and school assignment depend on the exact address, so check them with the county and the school district for any home you get serious about. For Williamson County, the [property search](https://www.williamsoncounty-tn.gov/2099/35739/Property-Data-Search) is a place to start.

I keep local figures for the I-65 corridor on the [market data page](/market-data).

## A reasonable next step

So, is now a good time to buy? The data shows a market in the balanced range that has been cooling, with a mortgage rate that makes the monthly payment a real factor. Whether that works for you comes down to your budget, your timeline and the home itself.

If you want to talk it through, fill out the [Get Matched form](/buy#form). I'll schedule a call, and you'll be talking with me within 48 hours. You can also reach me through the [contact page](/contact) with questions first. Either way, there's no obligation to make a move.

faq.q: Is now a good time to buy a home in Nashville?
faq.a: It depends on your finances, timeline and the specific home. Redfin showed 5.3 months of supply for Nashville as of 2026-08-31, which falls in the balanced range of 4 to 6 months.

faq.q: What are mortgage rates right now?
faq.a: Freddie Mac reported a 30-year fixed average of 7.28% for the week of 2026-10-01, via FRED. Rates change weekly, and your own rate depends on your lender and your finances.

faq.q: Are Nashville home prices going down?
faq.a: Redfin reported a Nashville median sale price of $477,500 as of 2026-08-31, down 0.1% from a year earlier. That describes the past, and nobody can reliably predict where prices go next.

faq.q: Should I wait for mortgage rates to fall before buying?
faq.a: Waiting is a bet in either direction, since nobody can reliably predict rates. The costs of waiting, such as rent paid, price changes or losing a home you wanted, are real even if easy to overlook.

faq.q: How much should I budget for closing costs?
faq.a: Closing costs typically run 2 to 4 percent of the purchase price, plus earnest money and moving costs. Your Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure show the actual figures for your loan.
